• Scientific name: Clavularia viridis
  • Common names: Palm tree polyp, Clove polyps, Octocoral, Naga-umizuta, Green star polyp coral, Eight Tentacle Polyps, Encrusting Polyps
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Keeping: Easy; propagation: Easy
  • Lighting: medium to high; water flow: moderate to strong
  • Salinity (SG): 1.021–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic
  • Placement: bottom to middle
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Toxicity: no
  • Invasive: yes (under optimal conditions)
  • Temper: peaceful
  • Colours: green, brown, purple, pink, cream and white, with contrasting colours (blue, green or yellow) at the centre of the oral disc

Choose a specimen that is healthy and lively, and avoid ones with drab coloration or a jelly-like substance on the body.

Palm tree polyp is one of the popular marine corals and rarely causes many problems in a reef aquarium. It is relatively hardy and will thrive for several years in a saltwater tank as long as optimal, stable conditions exist.

Clavularia viridis is a stoloniferous, colonial soft coral of the family Clavulariidae, native to the Indo-Pacific reef region. It is widely distributed in the Red Sea, South Africa, Korea, Palau, Guam, New Guinea, the Great Barrier Reef, the Indo-Pacific region and India (Andaman and Nicobar Islands).

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia; Phylum Cnidaria; Class Anthozoa; Order Alcyonacea; Family Clavulariidae; Genus Clavularia; Species Clavularia viridis.

This soft coral occurs at depths of up to 19 m and usually colonizes other marine coral species. It mainly grows on rocky areas and hard surfaces, attaching to them and spreading across to form a mat.

Although present throughout reefs, it mainly occupies the back and front reef slopes and the shallowest parts of the reef zones with tidal currents. According to the study, palm tree polyps are mostly found in areas with strong currents or wave action.

Palm tree polyp suits both small and large aquariums, given the potential size of the colony. The recommended minimum tank size is 10 gallons (40 litres). It can also be kept in nano aquariums if regularly trimmed.

To ensure optimal growth, health and longevity, provide ideal and stable water conditions. Keep temperature, pH, hardness, salinity and mineral composition at the correct levels and make any adjustments carefully.

Perform regular partial water changes — ideally 20% (monthly), 10% (weekly) and 5% (weekly) — to maintain excellent water quality and replenish depleted trace elements.

Palm tree polyp is a moderate to fast-growing coral that tends to branch out and grow over nearby corals, so keep an eye on it. To prevent this, mount the coral on a separate rock rather than on the main rockwork. Adding calcium and other mineral supplements is vital for its proper health and development.

Under optimal conditions palm tree polyps can be invasive, so ideally keep them confined to a particular area. Generally clove polyps are not invasive, but there are about 70 different species and how a given one behaves is never certain. They are very easy to remove from the tank: simply peel them back.

They do well on rocks, preferably in the low or middle sections of the reef aquarium, where they receive bright lighting and where the flow points towards them.

Some people put aggressive corals (such as frogspawn or torch corals) along the perimeter of the palm tree polyp. They will sting it away and prevent any expansion, but this may stress the coral until it melts away.

• Temperature: 22–27 °C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4 (standard reef aquarium pH)
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Salinity: specific gravity 1.021–1.025
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1200–1300 ppm
  • Salinity: 1.023–1.025
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm
  • Phosphates: < 0.05 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm
  • Nitrates: 5–10 ppm

Lighting: provide moderate to high intensity with quality LED aquarium lights, incandescent bulbs or even metal halides. Make sure the light output is enough to penetrate the water and reach the various areas of the aquarium. Maintain a standard photoperiod of about 8–10 hours daily.

Water flow: moderate to strong flow helps carry organic matter and plankton to the mouths of the polyps and equally carries waste material and detritus away from their bodies. Make sure the flow is not so strong that it damages the polyps.

Palm tree polyp feeds through photosynthesis, thanks to a mutually beneficial symbiotic relationship with marine algae called zooxanthellae. A wide variety of tropical hard and soft corals harbour symbiotic dinoflagellates (Symbiodinium spp.), broadly known as zooxanthellae, in their endodermal cells; according to the study, they transfer more than 90% of their photosynthetically fixed carbon to their host. The coral hosts the zooxanthellae in its tissue, offering shelter and protection, and in exchange the zooxanthellae enable photosynthesis and provide sustenance.

It also filter-feeds, absorbing dissolved organic matter from the water column. A sure way to ensure enough nutrition is supplemental feeding with meaty foods such as:

  • zooplankton
  • phytoplankton
  • reef roids, etc.

Do not give pieces of food that are too big. Make sure the food is finely crushed and mixed with aquarium water before feeding it to the coral with a feeding tool such as a turkey baster or pipette.

  • Photosynthetic: yes
  • Diet type: micro-plankton
  • Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a week

Palm tree polyp is a relatively peaceful and reef-compatible species. It is sturdy and can withstand mild scuffles and the chemical warfare of other marine corals; its retractable polyps help it cope with poor or harsh conditions.

As a mat-like encrusting coral, it can comfortably grow over a neighbouring coral. It is therefore recommended to place it on an isolated rock or keep a spacing of about 15 cm or more.

  • Peaceful: yes
  • Toxicity: no
  • Invasive: yes (under very favourable conditions)

This soft coral reproduces both sexually and asexually.

  • Sexually: male and female gametes are released into the water (spawning), followed by fertilization and the formation of planula larvae. The larvae are first free-swimming, but later develop and settle on sediments, undergo metamorphosis into polyps, then form a colony and continue to grow.
  • Asexually: by budding or by detaching part(s) of the body through fragmentation, which grows individually and forms a new colony.

Palm tree polyp is a soft coral with eight tentacles borne on several extended, tubular polyps arising from a thin plate-like or membranous basal stolon. The tentacles have feathery margins (pinnae), about 20 mm long and up to 3 mm in diameter, and become thicker toward the tips.

Colours vary from fluorescent green, brown, purple and pink to cream and white, with contrasting colours (blue, green or yellow) at the centre of the oral disc.

The polyps sit in tubular stalks (calyces) growing up to 5 cm tall. In nature a colony can reach a huge size, more than 1 m in diameter. When attached to rockwork or the substrate it forms an encrusting mat, with colonies connected at the base by stolons or thin membranes. It grows fast and is sessile; it may remain isolated on one rock for long periods.

Common problems

Brown jelly: a common disease of many corals including Clavularia species, characterized by a jelly-like brown mass that appears to float on the surface of the coral. It can be caused by poor water quality or tissue damage, can lead to rapid tissue necrosis and can spread to other corals in the tank. Solution: remove the sick coral from the tank, scrub off and siphon any visible brown jelly, treat the coral with an iodine dip (15 ppt), then keep it in a quarantine tank until it recovers before returning it to the main tank. Do not overdose; follow the instructions on the bottle based on your tank size.

Does not open (1): if it stays retracted for a few days after introduction to a new system, the coral is still shocked. Solution: check and adjust the water flow and lighting, as it can react this way if either is too strong or too weak. Then give it a few more days to adjust.

Does not open (2): sometimes palm tree polyps stop opening after a few months of normal behaviour, in many cases because of detritus and/or algae gathered inside the tentacles. Solution: clean with a turkey baster and tweezers if necessary, and keep the mat they grow from clean.

Fragging

Reef aquarists can divide the coral into several parts to propagate it. The process is simple:

  • Locate the tubular stalks.
  • Cut the polyp towards its base (stolon) with a sharp blade or scalpel; precision matters to prevent losses.
  • Gather the newly cut frags.
  • Disinfect them in an iodine solution and attach each to a coral frag plug with a quality cyanoacrylate gel.
  • Place each one in the reef tank, preferably at isolated spots in central tank areas where they will not be disturbed by curious or hostile tank mates.

A safer way that avoids cutting and stressing the coral is to put some rocks or plugs at its base. With time the polyps will spread their long tentacles and attach to the other surface.
